processing: Leaves of luobuma are hand-picked and dried. Details of the drying are seldom published and vary by producer.
harvest_season: Leaves are picked in summer. Hand-picking of premium wild leaf is reported to run for only about 15 days, in the morning and early afternoon.
appearance_dry: Dried narrow leaves in muted green, whole or broken.
appearance_liquor: Typically a light yellow-green, as with other dried-leaf infusions.
taste_profile: Little reliable tasting description exists; as with other dried-leaf herbal infusions, expect a plain herbal, vegetal cup.

brewing.notes: A general starting point for dried-leaf infusions, not a documented traditional method. Adjust to taste.

vintage_note: Not sold by vintage in any strict way. As is usual for dried-leaf herbal infusions, buy the most recent summer's leaf and drink it within a year or so. Wild-picked lots from the Yuli area are marketed as the premium, but that label is hard to check.
description:
Luobuma is a tough desert shrub, Apocynum venetum, and this is an infusion of its leaves, not tea plant. Its deep roots and tolerance of drought and salty ground are why it is planted to hold sand along the Taklamakan's edge.

The leaves are picked by hand and dried. Yuli County in southern Xinjiang is the main name here, with wild stands plus plantations. Little is published on the finer points of processing.

The taste is thinly documented too, so treat any poetic tasting notes with care. Brew it as you would any dried leaf herb: hot water, a few minutes, then adjust.

Claims that Xinjiang desert leaf is the best are promotional and untested, so buy for a recent harvest and clean smell. Luobuma is sold with many health promises; it is a plant with real activity, so anyone on medication should ask a doctor before making it a daily drink.
history:
Little is documented about the early history of luobuma as a drink. It does show up in folk culture: a saying listing the eight oddities of Dunhuang in Gansu includes the line that everyone loves luobuma tea.

Its recent story is about land and livelihoods. Yuli County in Xinjiang has grown luobuma as an ecological repair crop that also pays farmers, who take part in spring planting, summer leaf picking, autumn seed collecting and winter cutting. The plant also feeds local textile and health product industries.
